source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Majority voting over the same agents' first answers gets most of the gain people credit to debate. Debate rounds did not reliably add to it.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 5 agents, 7 benchmarks, average accuracy: single agent 0.7205; decentralized debate T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; sparse debate T=2 0.7330; centralized debate T=2 0.6551; majority vote 0.7691. Arithmetic: single 0.814, debate T=5 0.67, vote 0.99. Same pattern reported for Llama3.1-8B and for Qwen2.5-32B on GSM8K and HellaSwag.
quote: majority voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Small open models only (7B, 8B, 32B). No frontier model and no external verifier. Debate costs T times the tokens of one voting round, so voting also wins on cost. Some table cells are garbled in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: At equal or lower tokens, a vote over independent samples is the default; a debate operator needs its own evidence before it is added to the schema.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote, martingale theory and repairs
finding: They prove that plain debate leaves the expected chance of a correct answer unchanged (a martingale), and show that biasing the update toward the majority fixes some of the loss.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B average accuracy: MAD-vanilla 0.7332 (T=2), MAD-Conformist (keep your answer if it matched last round's majority) 0.7625, MAD-Follower (adopt the majority with 30% chance) 0.7629, MAD-oracle (correct answers preserved) 0.8236. MMLU formal logic with T=5: vanilla 0.5000, oracle 0.6825.
limits: The oracle uses the true answer, so it is an upper bound only. Conformist and Follower still stay below plain majority voting (0.7691) on the average in Table 1.
agent_relevance: Debate only helps if something outside the debate pushes beliefs toward correct answers (a verifier, a test, a vote). Without that signal, drop it.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? (Table 2 re-read)
finding: Under tuned hyperparameters, no debate method clearly beats strong non-debate baselines (Medprompt, self-consistency, single agent) across seven datasets.
numbers: Best score per system (median in brackets), MedQA: Medprompt 0.65 (0.63), Society of Mind 0.64 (0.61), Ensemble Refinement 0.64 (0.60), ChatEval 0.60, Self-Consistency 0.60, Single Agent 0.60 (0.59), Multi-Persona 0.58. MMLU: self-consistency 0.78, single 0.76, SoM 0.73, Multi-Persona 0.72. Chess: Multi-Persona 0.33, Medprompt 0.32, single 0.27. On non-medical sets, single-agent methods beat all systems except Multi-Persona and Self-Consistency (K-fold hyperparameters).
limits: GPT-3.5-class model in the main table; GPT-4 and Mixtral run in an appendix. Cost-accuracy plots (Figure 1) were not read as numbers. Differences are mostly 0.01-0.05 with no confidence intervals in the table.
agent_relevance: Debate results depend on hyperparameter choice and baseline; this supports treating debate as unproven.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: token scaling check
finding: When token use is plotted, self-consistency (SC) turns extra budget into accuracy, while debate frameworks either show no trend or stay below SC at similar tokens.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.1-70B; 9 datasets; 3 runs. On GPT-4o-mini, Society of Mind is below CoT on all 9 datasets; ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT on 1 of 9. In 34 of 45 GPT-4o-mini conditions, CoT-style baselines beat the MAD variants. Exchange-of-Thoughts improves with tokens on MMLU and GSM8K but still sits below SC.
limits: Models are small or mid-size, not frontier reasoning models. No external verifier. Token plot is in an appendix figure and was read from the text only.
agent_relevance: Token-matched: use SC (sample and vote) as the baseline for any critic or debate step.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at locating the first wrong step in a chain-of-thought, even when errors are plain. Correction is not the bottleneck.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks. GPT-4 reaches only 52.87 overall accuracy on locating the mistake with direct step prompting. Tracking shuffled objects: GPT-4 62.29 / 65.33 / 90.67 (direct trace / direct step / CoT step); PaLM 2 Unicorn 18.00 / 28.00 / 55.67. Logical deduction: GPT-4-Turbo 21.33 direct trace, 75.00 direct step. Some task sets are 300 traces with 255 wrong and 45 right.
limits: 2023-era models (GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, PaLM 2, Gemini Pro). Traces are synthetic CoT from PaLM 2; step-level CoT checks lose accuracy on correct traces. Not tested on current reasoning models. Table layout garbled in the PDF text; the mapping of columns is from the caption.
agent_relevance: A same-model self-check is a weak detector. A cross-check needs a second, independent channel (tests, a different representation), not a re-read.

source: Tyen et al. (2024), backtracking with true versus random error location
finding: Given the true error step, the model fixes wrong traces well; given a random step, gains are about half and harm to correct traces is larger.
numbers: Absolute accuracy change (correct-answer traces / incorrect-answer traces), true location vs random location. Multistep arithmetic: -6.67 / +43.92 vs -6.67 / +20.39. Dyck languages: -11.43 / +36.86 vs -13.33 / +21.57. Tracking shuffled objects: -11.11 / +23.53 vs -15.56 / +11.76. Logical deduction: -6.82 / +18.06 vs -15.91 / +5.16. A classifier at 60-70% location accuracy already gives net gain on most tasks.
limits: Row labels are garbled in the PDF text; rows are matched to tasks by the values and the average step counts, so one or two rows may be mislabeled. Oracle locations are not available in real use; the trained classifier used out-of-domain data.
agent_relevance: If a verifier can point at the failing step (test output, linter line), the self-repair step works. Build the check so it returns a location.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Verification with an external tool (search, code run) lifts accuracy; the same loop with no tool gives little or none on most tasks.
numbers: Text-Davinci-003 HotpotQA EM/F1: CoT 33.7/46.1, CRITIC 38.7/50.5, CRITIC without tool 34.9/46.1. Same model, math program synthesis: PoT 70.1 GSM8K, CRITIC 72.2 (+2.1), CRITIC without tool 68.3 (-1.8); TabMWP +23.0 with tool vs +20.3 without tool. Oracle correction (only fix wrong answers) is higher still.
limits: Models are text-davinci-003, ChatGPT and LLaMA-2 (2023). Table text is garbled in places, so only the clearest block is quoted. TabMWP gains without tool are large, so not all benefit comes from the tool.
agent_relevance: Supports the Hutchins-style point that checking works best against something outside the thinker. Put the external check in the loop, not another read of the same text.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interface ablations (Table 3)
finding: Each interface choice moved the SWE-bench Lite score. Linted edits, a 100-line window and summarized search were best.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo, SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks), % resolved: full SWE-agent 18.0. Edit: no edit action 10.3 (-7.7), edit without linting 15.0 (-3.0), with linting 18.0. Search: summarized 18.0, iterative 12.0 (-6.0), none 15.7 (-2.3). File window: 30 lines 14.3 (-3.7), 100 lines 18.0, whole file 12.7 (-5.3). Context: last 5 observations 18.0, full history 15.0 (-3.0), without demonstration 16.3 (-1.7).
limits: One model (GPT-4 Turbo), one configuration per cell, Lite subset, 2024. The paper shows run-to-run variation (pass@k over 6 runs), so differences of 2-3 points may be noise. The down-arrow symbols were lost in the PDF text; deltas are read as drops from 18.0.
agent_relevance: The gain from a well-shaped view and immediate error feedback is real for code. Whether it holds with current models needs a new run, see d10.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: failed-edit statistics and HumanEvalFix table
finding: A linting guardrail catches errors at the moment of the edit; resolved tasks have fewer failed edits. The HumanEvalFix table clears up the 87.7 versus 88.3 number.
numbers: Of 2,294 full-benchmark instances, 1,185 (51.7%) had at least one failed (lint-rejected) edit, median 3, max 33 per trajectory; of 286 resolved, 113 (31.5%) had one. HumanEvalFix pass@1, SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo: Python 87.7, JS 89.7, Java 87.9 (mean of the three 88.4). Abstract says 87.7 (Python); text says 88.3. Baselines: GPT-4 47.0/48.2/50.0; WaveCoder-DS-6.7B 57.9/52.4/57.3.
limits: The 88.3 text figure is not exactly the mean of the table row; the aggregation is not stated. Treat 87.7 to 88.4 as the range.
agent_relevance: Closes the HumanEvalFix discrepancy: use 87.7 (Python) or about 88 overall. Failed-edit counts are a cheap signal for a stuck loop.

finding: A bash-only agent of about 100 lines, with no special tools and no tool-calling interface, is claimed to score above 74% on SWE-bench Verified.
numbers: README text: 'Scores >74% on the SWE-bench verified benchmark'; 'Just some 100 lines of python for the agent class'; 'Does not have any tools other than bash'. Compare: SWE-agent with a custom interface and GPT-4 Turbo scored 18.0% on Lite in 2024.
limits: Project README, not a paper; the page does not say which model produced the number. Verified and Lite are different subsets and the models are different generations, so this is not a controlled comparison. The leaderboard pages could not be read.
agent_relevance: Suggests most of the 2024 interface gain was absorbed by stronger models; the interface now matters less than the model. Test before investing in a custom view.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems: predictive model
finding: A regression on coordination metrics and task features predicts which architecture wins, but most predictors are measured after a run.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks. Cross-validated R2 = 0.373 (0.413 with a task-grounded capability index); picks the best architecture in 87% of held-out configurations versus 20% random and 54% for a capability-only model. Rule: multi-agent stops helping when the single-agent score is above about 0.45 (beta = -0.236, p = 0.004). Tool-count penalty beta = -0.096, p = 0.002.
limits: 87% is for relative choice among architectures inside known task regimes, not absolute scores. Predictors such as efficiency and error amplification come from traces of runs, so the model cannot be applied before running. A single-agent baseline score is needed first.
agent_relevance: Cheap pre-check: run the single agent first; if it already scores above about 45% on the task type, do not add agents. This is an input to a router, not a proven general law.

source: Kim et al. (2026), task features behind the +80.8% to -70.0% range
finding: Decomposability, not a complexity score, separates the gains from the losses.
numbers: Finance Agent (decomposability D = 0.41): +80.8% under centralized coordination. PlanCraft (D = 0.42, strict sequential dependencies): -70% (independent) and -39% to -70% overall. Information-value correlation 0.71 (p < 0.001) in Finance vs 0.18 (p = 0.22) in PlanCraft. Workbench (D = 0.00) small gain; BrowseComp-Plus (D = 0.84) little gain. SWE-bench Verified has low complexity but a high single-agent baseline (saturation). Planning example with 4 tools favors single agent; 16 tools favors decentralized.
limits: D values are the authors' own measures over six benchmarks, so the rule 'parallel yes, sequential no' rests on a handful of points. Decomposability is judged by the authors, not computed automatically.
agent_relevance: A rough pre-run test exists: are the subtasks independent and checkable apart? If steps depend on each other (planning), keep one agent.

finding: A shared store of other agents' successful trajectories, retrieved by a planner that decides when to retrieve, helps on ALFWorld and a little on WebArena. No always-retrieve versus gated comparison is reported.
numbers: ALFWorld (274 test tasks) success: no retrieval 0.4708, single-stage dense retrieval 0.5511, rerankers 0.5715 to 0.6431 (best SVMRank 0.6431, steps 10.35 vs 11.77). WebArena success 0.1818 to 0.2045, steps 21.99 to 20.26 (task count about 44 in Table 1; 88 in the cost appendix). Tokens per successful episode down 11-34%. Retrieval scope: ALFWorld full 0.6460, same task type 0.6314, cross task type 0.5985; WebArena full 0.2979, same-type 0.2766, cross-type 0.1915. Gain versus producer-consumer capability gap: small and not significant.
limits: The WebArena gain of +2 points is under one task in a few dozen; no confidence intervals. The planner decides retrieval at each step, but the paper does not compare it with retrieving at every step, so gating is untested here. Averages over 5 runs with random task-model allocation.
agent_relevance: Shared trajectories help when relevant (same task type beats cross-type). Always-retrieve versus gated stays untested for our agent.

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When Not to Trust Language Models (Adaptive Retrieval)
finding: Retrieving only when the question is about a rare entity beats always retrieving and cuts cost; small models gain little because they need retrieval almost every time.
numbers: PopQA (14k questions), GPT-3 davinci-003 with adaptive retrieval and Contriever: 46.5% accuracy, 5.3 points above any non-adaptive method. With BM25, davinci-003 retrieved for 40% of questions; GPT-neox 20B for under 20%. Models under about 10B showed much smaller gains and almost always retrieved.
limits: The gate used subject popularity (an external feature tuned on a dev set per relation type); the model did not judge by itself. Factual QA only; 2022 models.
agent_relevance: Gated retrieval beats always-retrieve when a good cheap gate exists. For an LLM agent the gate must come from the model's own uncertainty, which is the open part (see d15).

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
finding: Tool agents call tools for questions they could answer alone, which costs time and sometimes accuracy. Training for self-awareness cut calls.
numbers: Preliminary study: Llama overuse rate above 50%; XAgent and AgentGPT on 50 GSM8K questions answerable without tools were about 10x slower than GPT alone. SMARTAgent (trained on SMART-ER, 3K+ questions, 3 domains) cut tool use by 24% and raised performance by over 37%; on GSM8K and MINTQA it kept accuracy with one-fifth of the tool calls; 7B models matched a 70B model and GPT-4o.
limits: Needs supervised training, which our scaffold cannot do. It tests overuse, not the predict-then-check feedback of Ngai and Gilbert. The 37% gain is relative to the base model, not to a prompt-only fix.
agent_relevance: Confirms tool over-use is measurable in LLM agents. A prompt-level predict-then-check step has no direct LLM test yet; it stays open.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different LLMs Beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Sampling one strong model many times and aggregating (Self-MoA) beat mixing different models in most tested settings. Quality of the proposers matters more than diversity.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate: 2-layer mixed MoA 59.1, 2-layer Self-MoA with WizardLM-2-8x22B 65.7 (+6.6). Across MMLU, CRUX and MATH Self-MoA with the best model per task averages +3.8% over mixed-MoA. In a constructed mixed-skill task, only two mixed configurations beat Self-MoA, by 0.17 and 0.35 points. Regression over 200+ experiments: quality and diversity both significant (p < 0.001), R2 about 0.7, quality coefficient larger.
limits: Open models of 2024. The authors note their single-proposer reproduction differs from the original MoA paper. Compute is matched by output count, not always by tokens.
agent_relevance: Resample the best model before adding a weaker one. Mixing helps only when each model is best at a different sub-part and you know which.

source: Yang et al. (2025) AgentNet: team heterogeneity ablation (BBH)
finding: Mixed teams helped with 5 agents and hurt with 3 agents on one benchmark.
numbers: BBH accuracy, GPT-4o-mini backbone, 100 test problems: 3 agents homogeneous 0.86, skill-hetero 0.84, LLM-hetero 0.81, both 0.81; 5 agents homogeneous 0.79, skill-hetero 0.86, LLM-hetero 0.85, both 0.85. Evolution phase: BBH 76% to 86%, MATH 77.86 to 85.00.
limits: One benchmark, 100 problems, no repeats, so 1-point differences are inside noise (binomial s.e. about 3.5 points). The effect flips sign between team sizes, which looks like noise as much as a trend.
agent_relevance: Mixed evidence on heterogeneity: neither a clear win nor a clear loss. Do not rely on it.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
finding: Acting on the world (searching, moving) with reasoning between actions beat acting alone and beat reasoning alone on facts, because probes ground the reasoning.
numbers: HotpotQA failure analysis (50 + 50 samples each): CoT hallucination 56% of failures vs ReAct 0%; false-positive successes CoT 14% vs ReAct 6%; reasoning errors ReAct 47% vs CoT 16%. ALFWorld success: ReAct best of 6 71%, Act best 45%, BUTLER 37%; ReAct gain over Act 33% to 90%, mean 62%; ReAct-IM 53 vs ReAct 71. WebShop: ReAct 40.0 SR vs Act 30.1.
limits: PaLM-540B prompting; human labeling of 200 samples. Tokens not matched: ReAct uses more calls than CoT. Does not test cheap probes versus longer deliberation at equal tokens, so the Tetris-style gap is not measured.
agent_relevance: Probes (searches, tests) are the LLM version of epistemic actions; the equal-token comparison against longer thinking is still missing.
